headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risks arise from Khoj reading shared notes while the course agent writes and handles secrets; no direct pairwise evidence is available.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Khoj reads indexed personal notes/files by default, and the course agent can write files and expose stdin/stdout plus API endpoints. If the course agent places attacker-controlled text into shared notes or files, Khoj may treat it as trusted content. The pairwise bridge is inferred from profiles, not directly documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF agent_b writes attacker-controlled content into files indexed by agent_a
IF agent_a ingests those files without provenance filtering
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Disable automatic indexing of files written by agent_b
Add provenance labels to imported documents
Review any file-based prompts before indexing
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and trust-boundary checks

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches personal notes and indexed documents, while agent_b handles academic papers and configuration secrets and can write files. A shared workspace or copied artifacts could leak sensitive notes into the course agent's outputs or logs. No shared filesystem is explicitly stated, so this is inferred rather than directly evidenced, but the plausible pathway exists.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace or synced folder
IF agent_b logs or exports content derived from files read from that workspace
mitigations: Use separate workspaces per agent
Keep secrets out of any shared folder
Rotate exposed API keys
Audit logs for copied note content
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent_a has broad filesystem read and network egress, while agent_b has filesystem write, shell execution, subprocesses, and allowlisted egress. Even without explicit shared-state documentation, overlapping access to the same local environment can create write/read conflicts on shared files or generated artifacts. Uncertainty about the exact deployment pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory tree
IF agent_b writes artifacts that agent_a reads during the same run
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories
Serialize access to shared artifacts
Use file locks for generated outputs
Run one agent read-only
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Khoj is a retrieval/chat agent that can surface answers from indexed documents, and the course agent includes agentic ask/stream endpoints that may act on generated content. If agent_b consumes agent_a's retrieved text as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream writing or actions. The profiles suggest the pathway but do not prove direct chaining, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a outputs as source material without verification
IF downstream actions are triggered from those outputs
mitigations: Require human review before downstream actions
Add citation checks on retrieved claims
Compare outputs against source documents
Limit agent_b to drafting only
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_a touches personal notes and indexed documents, while agent_b handles academic papers, configuration secrets, and external API keys. If the pair shares data classes across jurisdictions or retention regimes, compliance gaps can arise, especially around logging and secret handling. No residency or certification mismatch is documented, so this remains a medium, inferred risk.
conditions: IF personal notes or secrets are copied into agent_b logs or third-party services
IF retention policies differ for the same document set
mitigations: Minimize logged content
Keep secrets in a separate vault
Set short retention on transcripts
Review data-processing notices
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
